Maladaptive Strategies.value: I detach myself from the memories
I keep myself constantly surrounded by people so I am never alone with my thoughts
Being alone in a room or building

Memory.value: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.

vignette: Edward Vance had been fifty-two when the last night of the physical abuse caught him entirely off guard. He had come to believe that his partner’s anger was a weather system, something that passed, but that evening his partner’s hands had gripped his shoulders, pinning him against the kitchen wall, and Edward felt his body surrender to a weight that left him gasping. What frightened him most was the sudden, total loss of control; his limbs felt heavy, his voice stuck in his throat, and the floor seemed to tilt as the blows landed, not with fury alone, but with a cold, methodical force. He had never been struck by a man before, and the memory of that night arrived in his mind not as a flowing story but as a series of photographs. He saw the spilled wine, the darkening bruise on his ribs, the exact angle of his partner’s raised fist, and whenever the moment returned, he could taste the sharp tang of red wine and stale tobacco that had lingered in the room. When he tried deliberately to pull the memory forward, he found it difficult to access, as though it were locked behind a pane of glass. Now, at fifty-four, Edward’s office as a civil servant in the municipal building had become a quiet stage where the past kept surfacing. During a Tuesday briefing, a male colleague leaned over his desk to point at a ledger, his hand resting heavily on Edward’s shoulder. Edward’s breath caught. Being alone with men still made his pulse quicken, and the lack of control he had felt that night now echoed in the way he hesitated before speaking, as if waiting for someone else to take charge of the room. Over the following months, habits formed without his conscious direction. He began avoiding being alone in a room or building, preferring instead to keep his office door propped open and his desk chair angled toward the hallway. He discovered that constant socialising worked; he stopped taking lunch in silence, instead lingering in the breakroom with clerks and administrators, talking over file folders and printer hum while his thoughts moved alongside them. He went to the men’s club on Fridays, attended city council receptions, and remained surrounded by people. Yet the avoidance had consequences. He slept alone now, but not in the way he used to; he had retreated to the guest bedroom, then to a spare office cot, and eventually to the municipal lodging upstairs when late paperwork demanded it. Sleeping alone or in an unfamiliar place no longer felt like rest but like exposure. A hotel corridor could leave him pacing, his hand on the doorframe, certain that any moment a man might appear, and the floor might tilt again. His work held steady; he still filed reports, still sat through audits, still nodded at the mayor’s greetings. But the reluctance to occupy empty spaces, the way he kept his phone on speaker during evening drives, the careful distance he maintained from male colleagues’ physical gestures, had begun to limit his evening availability. He declined a solo review assignment, the hotel room feeling too wide, and instead spent those nights in the municipal building, surrounded by the low hum of security guards and cleaning staff. Edward had come to believe that his body still kept score of that kitchen night. When his partner left in the autumn, Edward stayed, and the quiet of the house settled around him, his symptoms holding steady. He noticed how the taste of red wine would rise in his mouth during morning briefings, how photographs in the staff calendar made his shoulders stiffen, how the sight of a male coworker adjusting his tie or rolling up his sleeves could send him toward the doorway. His memory detachment was a steady practice; when the kitchen wall pressed inward, he simply looked away, letting the photographs settle behind the glass. What finally brought him to seek help was the night he woke at three a.m., alone in the guest room, convinced he was still pinned, his mouth full of that old wine, his mind holding steady the images of the event. He came to the clinic hoping to understand why his body still guarded him, and what he might do to live without the constant watchfulness that had settled over his days.
